:::{#thm-spectral}
#### Spectral theorem for symmetric matrices

If $\matr{A}$ is a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix (@def-symmetric-matrix)
with real entries,
then there are a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{Q}$ (@def-orthogonal-matrix)
and a $p \times p$ diagonal matrix $\matr{\Eigvals}$ (@def-diagonal-matrix)
with real diagonal entries $\eigval_1, \ldots, \eigval_p$ such that

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{p \times p}
= \underbrace{\matr{Q}}_{p \times p}\,
\underbrace{\matr{\Eigvals}}_{p \times p}\,
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{Q}}}_{p \times p}
$$

Each $\eigval_i$ is an eigenvalue of $\matr{A}$ (@def-eigenvalue),
and column $i$ of $\matr{Q}$ is an eigenvector of $\matr{A}$ for $\eigval_i$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-spectral-equivalent-form}
#### An equivalent form of the spectral theorem

The proof, by [induction](proof-writing.qmd#def-proof-by-induction) on $p$, is outside the scope of these notes;
see @banerjee2014linear [Chapter 11, Theorem 11.27, p. 349],
which states the result in the equivalent form
$\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q} = \matr{\Eigvals}$.
The two forms are equivalent because
$\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q} = \matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{I}_p$
(@rem-orthogonal-matrix-columns).
Multiplying $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Eigvals}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
by $\tp{\matr{Q}}$ on the left and by $\matr{Q}$ on the right gives

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q}
&= \tp{\matr{Q}}\paren{\matr{Q}\matr{\Eigvals}\tp{\matr{Q}}}\matr{Q}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q}}\matr{\Eigvals}\paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(regroup; matrix multiplication is associative)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_p\matr{\Eigvals}\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(} \matr{Q} \text{ is orthogonal)}
\\
&= \matr{\Eigvals}
&& \text{(multiplying by } \matr{I}_p \text{ changes nothing)}
\ea
$$

Multiplying $\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q} = \matr{\Eigvals}$
by $\matr{Q}$ on the left and by $\tp{\matr{Q}}$ on the right
gives back the first form:

$$
\ba
\matr{Q}\matr{\Eigvals}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&= \matr{Q}\paren{\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q}}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \paren{\matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}}}\matr{A}\paren{\matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}}}
&& \text{(regroup; matrix multiplication is associative)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_p\matr{A}\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(} \matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{A}
&& \text{(multiplying by } \matr{I}_p \text{ changes nothing)}
\ea
$$

For example, let
$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
and
$\matr{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$,
which is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{Q}$.
Then

$$
\ba
\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{A}\matr{Q}
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(move the scalars to the front)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 2 + 1 \cd 1 & 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 2 \\ 1 \cd 2 + (-1) \cd 1 & 1 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication, first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 + 1 & 1 + 2 \\ 2 - 1 & 1 - 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 \cd 1 + 3 \cd 1 & 3 \cd 1 + 3 \cd (-1) \\ 1 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd 1 & 1 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd (-1) \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 + 3 & 3 - 3 \\ 1 - 1 & 1 + 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

a diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ of $\matr{A}$
from @exm-eigenvalue on its diagonal.

:::
